speaker: Eric Jang
title: What rebuilding AlphaGo teaches us about self-play, RL, and future of LLMs - Eric Jang
question: In machine learning and reinforcement learning, why do scaling laws often fail when used to guide a system from scratch?
guest: A mistake I made initially when I had bugs around how MCTS labeling was working was collecting data with an expert policy, treating it as a supervised learning problem, and trying to identify scaling laws on those datasets. You can indeed plot curves that look clean, but if you are in a regime where your policy is not working well, you may just be studying scaling laws on bad data. One important implementation detail is that if you want to study a scaling laws problem, you have to have a setup where the data is good, the architecture is good, and there are no bugs, and then solve it there. Ex ante, I was not able to apply scaling laws to direct what to look at until I had the rest of the system working. That sounds obvious, of course you want a working, bug-free system before studying scaling, but where I actually tripped up was jumping into the science of studying the artifact before the artifact was working well enough to be studied.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Scaling laws often fail from scratch because they are empirical fits, not first principles. They describe how performance changes with compute, data, or parameters only after a system already works: the architecture, optimizer, hyperparameters, and data pipeline are well tuned and training is in a smooth power-law regime. They extrapolate along a known-good recipe; they don't tell you how to find that recipe.

Starting from scratch, you are outside those conditions. Early behavior is dominated by things the laws leave out, such as optimization instability, poor initialization, mis-set learning rates, and data quality. The fitted constants and exponents are also specific to a setup, so they transfer poorly to new architectures, tasks, or data distributions.

Reinforcement learning makes this worse. The agent generates its own data, so the distribution is non-stationary and depends on exploration. Bootstrapped targets, the deadly triad (function approximation, bootstrapping, and off-policy learning together), plasticity loss, and overfitting to early experience mean that simply adding parameters or more updates per sample often hurts unless specific stabilizers, such as normalization, resets, or regularization, are in place. Scale then amplifies existing flaws rather than fixing them.

This is from general knowledge; I did not run a search.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer:
Scaling laws are empirical fits over an already-stabilized training recipe, not universal guarantees. In machine learning, smooth power-law gains assume stationary, clean data and well-tuned hyperparameters across scales. When building a system from scratch, uncalibrated optimization, flawed architectures, or noisy data mixtures distort small-scale pilot runs and invalidate extrapolations. Moreover, scaling laws predict continuous proxy losses like cross-entropy rather than downstream task performance, which often emerges abruptly past scale thresholds, leaving small models with flat, uninformative signal.

These failures intensify in reinforcement learning from scratch because the agent generates its own non-stationary data. Without a competent initial policy or dense rewards, extra compute and parameters cannot solve cold-start exploration bottlenecks: larger networks still receive zero learning signal if random actions never uncover reward. Even after reward is discovered, shifting state distributions, bootstrapping errors, and plasticity loss frequently cause larger RL networks to destabilize and degrade unless specialized architectural and optimization interventions are established first.

noweb.answer: Scaling laws often fail when building a system from scratch because they describe the retrospective Pareto frontier of already-tuned pipelines, not how to stabilize a new one. Clean power laws only emerge once architecture, data curation, normalization, and hyperparameter transfer rules are well calibrated; in an unvalidated system, subtle bugs, optimization instabilities, or data bottlenecks dominate error, causing small-scale pilots to mispredict large-scale behavior. Small runs also frequently sit in noisy pre-asymptotic regimes below phase transitions where capabilities suddenly emerge, while smooth gains in surrogate losses like cross-entropy or temporal-difference error often fail to track downstream task success. In reinforcement learning, non-stationary data makes extrapolation even more fragile. Because the agent generates its own experience, sparse rewards, poor exploration, value overestimation, plasticity loss, or reward hacking can starve or corrupt the learning signal early on. Scaling compute or parameters cannot extrapolate a trend until the underlying exploration, credit-assignment, and optimization loops actually work.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Scaling laws are empirical curve fits, not first-principles theory. They only hold inside the regime where they were measured, and a system built from scratch usually starts outside that regime.

First, the fits assume a fixed recipe that already works. The architecture, optimizer, hyperparameters, data mix and stability tricks all have to be tuned before the power law appears. A new system hasn't settled any of these, and changing them shifts or breaks the curve.

Second, small-scale behavior is often "pre-asymptotic." Early points are noisy and dominated by transients and bottlenecks, so extrapolating from them can mislead badly. Broken power laws, sudden emergent abilities and phase transitions mean a smooth trend at small scale may not continue.

Third, the laws predict proxy metrics like loss, not the downstream capabilities you actually care about.

Reinforcement learning makes all of this worse. The training data comes from the agent's own changing policy, so the distribution isn't stationary. Exploration, reward sparsity and instability can stall or collapse training. Recent RL scaling work, such as Meta's 2025 ScaleRL study, found performance follows sigmoid-shaped curves whose ceiling depends on the recipe. So you need a stable, validated setup before extrapolation is reliable. Scaling laws are good for refining a working system, not for finding one.

models.answer: Scaling laws are empirical fits to a mature, well-tuned regime, not first-principles blueprints for building a system from scratch. When starting from scratch, small-scale runs are usually confounded by suboptimal hyperparameters, architectural flaws, data-pipeline bugs, or poor inductive biases; extrapolating from an untuned baseline projects the wrong slope and misallocates compute. Scaling laws also assume that the dominant bottleneck remains unchanged across orders of magnitude, yet larger runs routinely hit new failure modes—such as optimization instabilities, gradient explosions, precision limits, or data saturation—that are invisible at small scale. Moreover, scaling laws typically track smooth proxy objectives like cross-entropy loss rather than downstream capabilities, which can emerge discontinuously or plateau unexpectedly. In reinforcement learning, these issues are compounded by non-stationarity: because the policy generates its own training data, small agents often fail to cross exploration thresholds, suffer from plasticity loss, or exploit reward loopholes, meaning small-scale runs may never enter the regime where predictable scaling even begins.

In reinforcement learning, the agent’s behavior also determines what data it sees. An agent that rarely discovers a reward may gain little from more training, even if performance scales predictably once it learns to reach that reward. The scaling law can help estimate the payoff from additional compute within a tested regime. On its own, it cannot tell you how to get into that regime.
